title: Troubleshooting Clusters & Nodes
summary: NotReady nodes, component logs, static Pod manifests, kubelet checks, node debugging and kubeadm gotchas.

blocks.text: The investigator's first round is a roll call: is every ship (node) registered and **Ready**? A ship that lost its radio, or whose cargo officer (`kubelet`) died, shows `NotReady`; its health conditions turn **Unknown**, and the port hangs "unreachable" signs on it (taints). After five minutes its bays are evicted. `kubectl describe node` and `kubectl cluster-info dump` give the details.
First confirm every node you expect is registered and **Ready**. Then dig into any node that isn't.

kubectl get nodes
kubectl describe node <node-name>
kubectl get node <node-name> -o yaml
kubectl cluster-info dump        # detailed overall health
What a down node looks like (network cut, or a kubelet that died and won't restart):

items: Conditions `Ready`, `MemoryPressure`, `DiskPressure` and `PIDPressure` go to **Unknown** with the message that the kubelet stopped posting node status.
Its Pods are evicted after **five minutes** of NotReady.

blocks.text: In `-o yaml`, `status.daemonEndpoints.kubeletEndpoint` shows the kubelet port (10250 in the example).

For deeper clues, the investigator boards the machines and reads their logbooks. In the harbor office, the front desk, load planner and supervisors each keep a file under `/var/log`, such as `kube-apiserver.log`. On each ship, the cargo officer (`kubelet`) and the switchboard operator (`kube-proxy`) keep theirs. On systemd hosts, you may need `journalctl` instead of these files.
Going deeper means logging in to the machine. On systemd hosts you may need `journalctl` instead of these files.

Not every crew member works from a bay. The cargo officer (`kubelet`) and the crane (container runtime) work outside containers, so on systemd hosts they write to the ship's journal: `journalctl -u kubelet`. The front desk, load planner and supervisors usually live in pinned bays (static Pods), as the ledger often does, and those write files under `/var/log`. The switchboard operator typically rides every ship (DaemonSet).

items: The **kubelet and container runtime** don't run in containers. On Linux with systemd they write to **journald**: read with `journalctl -u kubelet`.
Without systemd they write `.log` files under `/var/log`.
The **API server, scheduler and controller manager** run in Pods, usually **static Pods**. etcd most commonly does too.
Components in Pods write files under `/var/log`, not the systemd journal.
kube-proxy, when used, typically runs as a **DaemonSet**.

blocks.text: journalctl -u kubelet
On the node itself, read the kubelet with `journalctl -u kubelet` (systemd) and the Pod-based components through their files under `/var/log`.

Pinned bays come from a folder the cargo officer checks regularly (`staticPodPath`, for example `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`). Drop a file in to start a bay; move it out to stop it. The front desk only sees a mirror copy, so deleting that mirror stops nothing. The officer reads every file not starting with a dot, so keep backups outside. When the front desk is silent, inspect the crane directly with `crictl`.
The kubelet itself runs static Pods from a directory set by `staticPodPath` in its config file. `/etc/kubernetes/manifests` is the example directory.

items: The kubelet scans the directory regularly. Add a file to start a Pod; move it out to stop it.
Each static Pod gets a **mirror Pod** in the API server. Deleting the mirror with kubectl does **not** stop the static Pod.
The kubelet reads **every** file not starting with a dot, whatever its extension. Keep backups such as `kube-apiserver.yaml.backup` **outside** the directory.

blocks.text: When the API server can't help, inspect containers on the node with crictl:

crictl ps
crictl logs <container-id>
# after editing kubelet config
systemctl restart kubelet

If a ship's cargo officer seems off duty, check on them directly: `systemctl status kubelet` and `journalctl -xeu kubelet`, then reload and restart the service. On ports built by the construction crew (`kubeadm`), the office's pinned bay files live in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`, and during upgrades the crew backs up those files and the ledger in `/etc/kubernetes/tmp`, ready for a manual restore.

systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -xeu kubelet
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart kubelet

items: kubeadm control plane nodes keep their component manifests in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`.
During upgrades kubeadm backs up manifests and etcd data under `/etc/kubernetes/tmp`, which you can restore by hand if rollback fails.

sections.heading: Shell on a node with kubectl debug

blocks.text: No gangway onto the ship (no SSH)? Send a debugging bay aboard with `kubectl debug node/<node-name>`. The ship's whole hold appears at `/host`, so logs like `/host/var/log/kubelet.log` are in reach. It shares the ship's network and processes but isn't privileged, so `chroot /host` fails without `--profile=sysadmin`. It can't board a ship that's already down. Delete the bay when done.
No SSH? Run a debugging Pod on the node:

kubectl debug node/<node-name> -it --image=ubuntu
# when done
kubectl delete pod <node-debugger-pod-name> --now

items: The node's root filesystem is at `/host`. Useful logs: `/host/var/log/kubelet.log`, `/host/var/log/kube-proxy.log`, `/host/var/log/containerd.log`, `/host/var/log/syslog`, `/host/var/log/kern.log`.
It shares the host IPC, network and PID namespaces but is **not privileged**, so `chroot /host` fails. Use `--profile=sysadmin` for privileges.
It won't work on a node that's down (network gone or kubelet dead).

blocks.text: Picture what breaks. If the front desk (`kube-apiserver`) goes down, nobody can start, stop or change bays, yet running work carries on. Lose the ledger's storage and the desk won't start healthy, while ships keep their bays. One ship down stops its bays; a faulty cargo officer means replicas start elsewhere. A radio split makes each side think the other sank. Spare offices, reliable storage and snapshots soften the blows.

rows: Can't stop, update or start Pods/Services; running workloads keep going unless they need the API
kube-apiserver won't start healthy; kubelets keep running existing Pods; manual recovery needed
No new Pods there; node marked unhealthy; replicas start elsewhere
Each side thinks the other is down

blocks.text: Mitigations listed: automatic VM restart, reliable storage for API server + etcd, a high-availability control plane (with HA etcd), periodic volume snapshots, and controllers plus Services in front of Pods.

When the construction crew (`kubeadm`) hits trouble, the investigator knows the usual suspects. `kubeadm init` hanging points to network trouble or crashlooping office containers; check with `crictl`. The phone directory (`coredns`) waits in Pending until the road contractor's network add-on arrives, and errors after that suggest a broken add-on. An `x509` error on your radio means a bad kubeconfig. A wrong ship address needs `--node-ip` and a kubelet restart.

rows: `kubeadm init` hangs waiting for the control plane
Network problems, or control plane containers crashlooping. Inspect them with the runtime (crictl)
Expected until you install a Pod network add-on
Pods in RunContainerError / CrashLoopBackOff / Error after the add-on
The network add-on is probably broken
`x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` from kubectl
Restart the container runtime, then rerun reset
kubelet picks the wrong node IP
Set `--node-ip`, then `systemctl daemon-reload` and `systemctl restart kubelet`

options.text: The kubelet reads both files, and the stale spec might win
options.explanation: No filtering by extension; same-named Pods give undefined behaviour.

options.text: None, the kubelet only reads .yaml files
options.explanation: It processes every file not starting with a dot.

options.text: The API server rejects both Pods
options.explanation: The kubelet creates static Pods itself.

options.text: The kubelet deletes the backup automatically
options.explanation: It doesn't.

questions.stem: True or false: Deleting a static Pod's mirror Pod with `kubectl delete pod` stops the static Pod.

options.explanation: The kubelet keeps running it; the mirror Pod comes back.
Correct. Remove the manifest from the static Pod directory to stop it.
